root.note: The word is from Nahuatl through Spanish, but the exact Nahuatl form is disputed. The popular ‘xocolatl = bitter drink’ is not found in early sources. Many experts now link the word with the wooden beater used to make the drink foam.

stages.meaning: also a sweet food in bars

history: Chocolate was first a drink. In Mexico and Central America, people made a bitter drink from cacao beans, often with chilli, and the Spanish brought it to Europe in the 1500s. English took the word chocolate from Spanish around 1600, and the first chocolate houses opened in London in the 1650s. Where the Spanish word comes from is less clear than many websites say. It is from Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, but the often-quoted form xocolatl, ‘bitter drink’, does not appear in early sources. Many experts now connect it with the wooden stick used to beat the drink. Chocolate bars are much younger: the first British one was made by Fry's in 1847.
historyEinfach: Chocolate was first a drink. It comes from Mexico. People made it from cacao beans. It was not sweet. The Spanish brought it to Europe. The word comes from the Aztec language, but we don't know exactly which word. Chocolate bars came much later, in the 1800s.

cognates.note: from Spanish cacao, from Nahuatl cacahuatl

elsewhere.text: Spanish passed the word on to the rest of Europe with small changes in spelling. Spanish chocolate is still also a thick hot drink, and churros con chocolate is a popular breakfast or snack.
